newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey, burned by Gulf War, eases pro-U.S. stance.
newsitem.headline: Turkey, burned by Gulf War, eases pro-U.S. stance.

text.p: NATO ally Turkey distanced itself on Friday from any role in U.S. air strikes on Iraq in a slackening of its support for the Gulf War coalition brought on by the harsh realities of life as Baghdad's neighbour.
Foreign ministry officials confirmed a call by Turkey's U.S. ambassador, Nuzhet Kandemir, for Washington not to let loose the military might it is ranging against Iraq.
"Ambassador Kandemir was expressing his own views without stepping out of line with the government's policy," a ministry official said.
The envoy on Thursday cautioned against possible U.S. air raids on Iraq and urged a softer, diplomatic approach to bring Baghdad back into the international community.
"We hope that these kinds of punitive strikes, particularly disproportionate ones, will not take place," Kandemir told journalists at a luncheon in Washington.
Other former coalition members, with the exception of Britain, have withheld backing for U.S. air raids.
"It is far better to have Iraq within the community of nations and to have them abide by the U.N. and international rules and procedures," Kandemir said.
Iraq says Turkey has given assurance that it would not let Turkey-based U.S. jets hit Iraq to punish President Saddam Hussein for defying Western-imposed no-fly zones.
Turkey fears a U.S. conflict with Iraq would ruin the already slim prospects of reviving a lucrative oil pipeline deal with Baghdad, and destabilise its sensitive southeastern border.
"Besides Iraq, the country that has suffered most from the treatment of Iraq is Turkey," said Sadi Erguvenc of the Foreign Policy Institute, a think tank close to the official line.

Turkey often rues its strong backing for the coalition that forced Saddam out of Kuwait in 1991, complaining that it has lost over $25 billion in trade with Iraq in six years of U.N. sanctions on Baghdad. Western diplomats say the figure is lower.

Ankara cut off a pipeline carrying Iraqi oil through its territory within days of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait and allowed U.S. planes to bomb Iraq from a joint Turkish-U.S. base in Turkey during the Gulf War.
But the pipeline, to the Turkish terminal of Yumurtalik, remains closed despite agreement at the United Nations to get Iraqi crude flowing again under a $2 billion oil-for-food deal.
The United Nations froze the deal -- dashing Turkish hopes of hefty transit revenues from the line -- after Saddam's troops took sides in Kurdish infighting in north Iraq last month.
Despite condemning Baghdad's involvement in the Kurdish feud, Turkish officials are privately pleased that Saddam has increased his influence in what was no-man's land in north Iraq.
Turkey had often complained that clashes between two Iraqi Kurdish groups had allowed the Turkish Kurd guerrillas to establish themselves in the mountainous region.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller has brought fire from many Arab countries, plus Russia and France, for suggesting a Turkish security zone in north Iraq to stop rebel border infiltration.
The pro-Baghdad Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) has united much of northern Iraq under its control after defeating rival Iraq Kurdish fighters earlier this week.
"(The situation in northern Iraq) is actually going quite well for Turkey," a Western diplomat said.

Turkey hosts a U.S.-led allied air force that patrols the no-fly zone over northern Iraq but it strongly opposes the founding of a Kurdish state there that might encourage separatist sentiments among its own restive Kurdish minority.
"The possibility of an American satellite state of Kurdistan being set up in northern Iraq is now off the agenda," left-wing nationalist leader Bulent Ecevit told a news conference.
